Phainon grimaces as the driver laughs, full, loud and satisfied.

“Don’t worry, I ask customers to rate me low all the time. People like you don’t really show up for high rated drivers, and I want the gossip more than I want some gold star on my app.” He says as the car door clicks, opening.

“Better make do on that promise, kid. Trust your senior on this, won't you?”

“We’ll see about that,” he says, shutting the car door. “I’ll tip you if we end up kissing. Our chat should still be accessible 24-hours after this ride.”

The driver grins straight at him, like he already knows what’s gonna happen.

“You better tip me regardless, and give me one star if it works out. You best be grateful to me, after, since I helped you snag a pretty damn good boyfriend. Good luck tonight, lover boy. Stay safe.”

And he drives off as Phainon huffs, stepping into his building. He’ll see if he ends up tipping tonight.

Waiting for Mydei to come home is like waiting for the other shoe to drop. The wait of an execution, the countdown for an inevitable doomsday clock.

Okay, maybe nothing that dramatic, but his heart is leaping out his chest while his face is stuck in forced nonchalance.

Phainon is in his room, pacing, thinking of how exactly he’ll explain this. He knows three things:

1. Mydei, unquestionably, has seen Phainon drool over his arms on camera. If he’s unlucky, Mydei could have also seen the other clip of Phainon blushing at the mere mention of his roommate.

2. Unless Mydei is choosing to be obtuse: he must know that Phainon is attracted to him. The clips are proof. Literal, undeniable proof of this.

3. Whatever reaction Mydei has or had must be strong enough that he’d walk out of the panel immediately. To chase after him? To meet back out with his mother? That part’s up in the air, but it was certain that he had some kind of visceral reaction to the news.

Phainon’s not sure what exactly that means for him , but all spelled out like this, it does make him worry. Is this really the time to confront this?

The door creaks open, and he freezes.

The thing about routines, is that once you’ve gotten used to them, it’s near impossible not to notice the slight differences in one’s habits. Their door, for example, has been creaky ever since they moved in. It was heavy, slightly too heavy for the frame, but just costly enough that they’d think twice to replace it.

In the end, it became a permanent fixture of their house.

Whenever one of them comes home, they’d knock the door first, twice, before creaking the door to enter. They’d do so as a prior warning, ensuring that no one would be spooked with the sound of their door scratching against the flooring.

Afterwards, they’d drop their keys by the side of the door, right on the holder they kept there, and the sounds of their shoe cabinet would accompany this routine.

Tonight, Mydei does none of that. What he hears instead is the furious stomping of a man who’s never broken routine before.

“HKS,” he growls out. “You ran away. Why?”

“Before you say anything!” Phainon raises his arms, trying for unthreatening, “you get to punch me. Or we can fight, whatever you want. I deserve it, I know, but-”

Mydei jumps at him. No, he lunges, tackling him to the ground, caging him in.

“Do you really know what you’ve done? Do you understand what’s just happened?”

“Um. You saw the clip?”

“Everyone saw the clip.”

“...And are you mad at what I said?” Phainon tries. He doesn’t know if he wants to hear his answer.

“Am I mad? Mad? Phainon, you confessed to me via TikTok. How the fuck did you expect me to respond?”

Mydei leaned in, the heat of him almost burning from where his hands caged either side of his head.

He could feel the slight warmth of him. Mydei always ran hotter than most, but he was uncharacteristically warm. He must’ve ran up the complex and through the halls to get here, working up a sweat.

He gulps. "I'm sorry if I made you uncomfortable-"

"Uncomfortable?"

"If you want to move out. If you ever want to move out because of this. I'll help you find a new place. And lease it. And. And whatever. I'll do it, okay? I'm sorry if I weirded you out."

Mydei leans down, slamming his palms on either side of his head once more.

"Don't even entertain that idea. You dare? You dare drop such a confession on me and leave me alone? I could not reply. I could neither reject nor accept you. What a coward you are, HKS. A Coward."

It is admonishment, not rejection. All the blood is rushing to his head, to his heart, pumping fast like a chase, like a hunt, like he's getting close to something once thought as unobtainable.

"Your mother," he says, "has she-"

"I've parted with her. I called a cab. Stop changing the subject and answer me. Did you mean what you said?"

“Mydei,” he repeats again. He needs an answer, he needs to know. Even if it burns him, even if he doesn't know what to do with himself after. This is Mydei, this is him. “Mydeimos. Are you mad at what I said?” (Are you mad at what I've done? Are you repulsed by me?)

“Are you kidding? Are you stupid? How much more do I have to spell it out!?” (Tell me. Tell me, please, while I still have the courage to ask.)

“And if I do? If I need you to tell me, to remind me, every day. Would you?” (Would you stay for this? For me?)

Mydei growls, backing away like he’s been burned. The tension sizzles in the air as Phainon sits up. Waiting. Watching.

“You are an idiot. A scoundrel. A Hyena in everything but form . ”

He says, and the punch he throws after feels almost like nothing compared to the weight of his next words. “Fight me. You don’t get to demand anything from me. Not like this.”

And Phainon could not do anything but oblige.

This wasn’t like the ring. Controlled, spacious. A place made for violence, sleek floors and safety bars and a first aid kit always in reach. Here, in the space they’ve carved as theirs, on their carpets and beholden to the walls that they call home, they fought, not like fighters, but like strangers.

It wasn’t the dance they’d go on when they box. Calculated trades and blows and jabs. Another form of routine, every step, another beat of familiarity.

No, this was wild. Phainon doesn’t know how it started, who's thrown the first punch after Mydei’s declaration, whose body ends where and whose leg is stuck on whose. They fought like a mess, like they’ve never fought each other before, not like this.

Sometime during their tousle, Phainon ends up on top of him, a mirror of the last time they’d boxed, both of them panting and tired from the exertion, from the thinking.

“Mydei,” he starts again. “I haven’t heard an answer.”

(Please. I don’t think I can wait.)

Mydei doesn’t respond.

Because this is unlike the gym, unlike the ring.

Mydei never loses, not really. He’s a better fighter than Phainon is, he knows that. The times when he wins are the times Mydei chooses to submit. And this time, he does not want to.

He slams his knee into Phainon’s stomach from where he lays on the ground. Phainon had no hope to dodge it at all. He hacks, and coughs, as Mydei tackles him once more, bringing him to the ground, firmly below him.

“A hundred wins.” He says. He does not smirk, nor is he triumphant and it dawns on him that this was more than a fight, more than a spar. "Loser takes the winner out," he simply says it as a reminder, a choice.

Phainon blinks dazedly. The side of his lip, he knows, is split. Probably the result of a punch he’d failed to dodge, or a kick he hadn’t paid attention to. Mydei, in contrast, looks only slightly out of breath. He’s heaving, purple marks on his neck and arms, bruises blooming from where he’d gotten contact.

He’s beautiful.

Even like this, Phainon thinks he loves him.

“Mydei,” he breathes. Just to say his name. Just to acknowledge that he’s here, that this, if nothing else, is real.

Mydei opens his mouth, then closes it, and before he can get anything out, Mydei crashes his lips onto his.

Phainon’s eyes widen, scrambling to reach out, to anchor himself, to anything. His hands hover around Mydei’s hips, his shoulders, his sides, unsure of where to hold him where his fists haven’t already. He doesn’t want to agitate his bruises.

Mydei growls against him, slotting himself against Phainon’s hands and arms where he hesitates. Phainon tastes like blood. Mydei, like honey. The split of his lip stings from where Mydeis canines scratch against it, but he cannot bring himself to mind.

It is intoxicating, warm, warm heat, from his mouth, from muscle, from his heart. From all of him, it is too much, yet not quite enough. Like the buzz of rum, of pomegranates, just enough to be enticing.

And in a moment too short for infinity yet too long for a second he pulls away. And Phainon is cold, not unbearably so, but cold enough to remember that for now, he is without heat.

“Dinner,” Mydei pants from above him, “Your treat, anywhere, anytime. You choose, I don’t care. Just take me somewhere nice, then ask me again, and make it right. I’ll answer yes, everytime, however many times you ask. You know I will– you know I would have.”

And he kisses him again, but it’s Phainon who pulls him down. And he thinks that this time, he might allow himself to take it.

“Wherever I want.” He echoes.

Can that be here? Can it be now?

“It’s late,” Mydei mutters against his lips, the heat of him never leaving his side.

Phainon’s hands take his wrist, trailing the tattoos that swirl just by the end of his palm, cool fingers sliding against his forearm onto the line of tendon, skin and muscle. Not unlike a cuff, not unlike a chain. Mydei shivers at the contact, entirely too warm for it. Phainon isn’t a selfish man. But maybe, he’s been denying this for far too long.

“You promised me anytime, and I haven’t eaten anything all day. Get changed. I’ll take you somewhere nice.”

“Are those your Wario shoes?” Mydei asks, eyeing Phainon’s choice in footwear.

“My favourite ones,” he smiles.

Mydei scoffs, looking away, a faint blush on his cheeks. “Just because I bought them for you doesn’t mean you have to keep them. I bought it as a joke. Aren’t you embarrassed?”

“Throwing out perfectly good shoes is unethical, Mydei. And besides, I only wear them on special occasions. Surely this is special enough?”

The only good restaurants that opened this late that’d accept them without reservation were high-end bars and the like. Phainon had googled expensive bars in the area, chosen a spot that had private booths, and decided on that.

When he’d called an uber, and matched with the same 3.2 rated man he had before, he had to begrudgingly tip him twice to stay quiet. The man’s wiggled eyebrows spoke more than any words.

“Nice night out for a date, isn’t it?”

“Shut up and drive.” Phainon hissed. Mydei raised his brow. “Please?” Phainon tacked on hurriedly.

The driver cackled, saluting, as he resumed their drive. Once they’d arrived, and Mydei stepped out the car, he’d pulled the same door-locking trick as he winked at Phainon, full of smugness.

“I see those bruises on his neck,” he wolf-whistled, “I said to kiss him, not maim the guy. You’re more forward than I thought, kid. Good job. I knew you had it in you.”

Phainon sputtered as a furious blush took hold on his face. “We haven’t done that! I only kissed him! Twice!”

The driver looked at him, smirking, before pulling his ear closer. “I got condoms in the back seat. Reach in if you need anyth-” And that was when Phainon quickly unlocked the door, left, and slammed it for good measure. He rated him one star, both times, and left a fat couple thousand credits as a tip.

But aside from the car ride, the dinner had been fine.

Mydei had dressed up, wearing a high turtleneck in a vain attempt to cover up his suspicious looking bruises, fitted black slacks and a black coat, to match. He’d tacked on his usual jewelry, bracelets and necklaces, with the addition of his signature, golden earrings.

On the other hand, Phainon was wearing the only truly put together outfit he had, which still looked odd when paired with Mydei’s all black ensemble.

He sported a white shirt, brown pants and a white flannel to tie it together. His injuries were mostly around his legs, chest, and stomach, so it wasn’t as pressing to wear something high. The most glaring difference, though, was in their choice of footwear, Mydei’s black and gold loafers against Phainon’s purple-yellow sneakers.

Mydei snorted as the waiter arrived, bringing their drinks. For Mydei, a blood orange spritz and Phainon, a gin and tonic. “You’re drinking tonight?” He raises his brow.

“Neither of us are driving,” he shrugged, “who knows? It might be an acquired taste.”

“What. You handle liquor worse than children do. The one time you tried beer in college, you threw up on Hyacine’s floor.”

“And I’m still a broke college student at heart,” Phainon said, hand to his heart, in one of the most expensive bars in Okhema, “but I’d like to think I’ve grown at least slightly since then.”

Mydei doesn’t respond, only shaking his head as he settles back into the booth.

The banter is nice. It’s welcome. A step back into routine, into something, somewhere more familiar. Phainon nudges his ankle, just to get a reaction out of him when Mydei seems to doze off prematurely. He usually doesn’t stay up this late, an early sleeper and early riser a part of the discipline ingrained within him.

Phainon scooches over so they’re sitting shoulder to shoulder, instead of facing each other, a much more familiar position for the both of them. Mydei is an amenable warmth on his right, the heat of him felt even through his layers of clothing.

He nudges him once more, just to get a reaction, and Mydei’s hand falls onto Phainon’s thigh to get him to stop his prodding.

“Aren’t you forgetting what we’re here for?”

“For dinner? For drinks? To spend time with each other, perhaps?”

Mydei gives him A Look, unimpressed, as he flicks his forehead. He leans against him, earring digging into Phainon’s shoulder, but he speaks not a word of protest.

How could he, when the bar’s low, golden lighting makes his eyeliner glitter like the sapphire of his earrings? His eyes, half-lidded and fluttering, stare at him under a sweep of lash. Devastatingly, the light shines warmth on the side of his cheek, his neck, the gold of his eyes and the shine of kiss-bitten lips.

“Quit staring. I can hear your brain from here. Turn it off.”

“I haven’t said anything!”

“You don’t need to. I already know.”

“Yeah?” Phainon challenges, “What could I be thinking of now?”

When mydei gazes up at him, slightly flushed, from the alcohol, from the lights, from the closeness of them this night, Phainon feels his heart leap out of his throat. “Me, of course,” a devastating smile, “likewise, I’m thinking of no one else.”

Tipsy Mydei is a menace .

“You’re drunk. Oh, titans, you’ve finished your drink already and haven’t eaten anything– no wonder you’re drunk! Alright, that’s enough of that, yep, okay. Stop- stop clinging to me, wait-”

If Mydei before was a weight on his side, this Mydei was a lion clinging on for dear life. Like Mufasa, maybe. And Phainon was Pride Rock.

“Mydei, I have water. Sober up, will you? This. This isn’t good for my heart.”

Mydei hand trails along his cheek, stopping just by his sun tattoo, just by the stuttering pulse on his neck, laughing soft as Phainon shivers. “I’m not nearly as drunk as you think I am, but the concern is touching, nonetheless. Come on now, get on with it. We have an agenda tonight, don’t we?”

“You can’t seriously expect me to confess while you’re drunk ?”

“Why not? I’ll remember. I know the limits of my body well. Ask me. I’ll still be yours by daylight.”

Who taught him this? Who taught Mydei to be smooth ?

Phainon gives in to the teenage urge to put his face into his hands and lie in the fetal position on the booth. He can feel his cheeks burning as he kicks his feet, giddy. He wants the ground to swallow him whole, yet he wants to immortalize this moment all the same.

“You’re a fiend. An absolute fiend. You say things that are bad for my heart. Do you not know how much I’ve wanted? How long I’ve waited for this? You can’t just. Just affirm it all, one night, out of nowhere. It’s not fair. I could’ve had this from the start?”

“You’ve never asked, and I’ve been waiting, for forever. I’ve told you this, at times, when you’re drunk and amenable. But you never listen. You rarely do.”

“What. What are you saying."

"I've confessed to you. Multiple times, while you were under the affects of alcohol. And you forget, in the mornings, every time."

"What? And you let me do that?”

Mydei shrugs, “Your sober self shirks off any acknowledgement of intimacy. What else was I supposed to do?”

“I don’t drink that often. I can’t possibly have done so much.”

“Phainon. My mother has insisted I gift you wine ever since your 21st birthday. Wine that you drink in the confines of our home, where no one but I am there to witness you. Believe me, I have tried confessing before. I have not found a way to get you to remember.”

“We could’ve been dating.”

“We’ve established that, yes.”

“And I’ve only realized that after inadvertently confessing via TikTok?”

“Heh. I suppose that’s true as well.”

“Fuck me.”

“I would not be opposed.”

“Fuck you , you can’t just say that.”

“I would also not be opposed. And I can just say that, because I’m sober and for once, you’re sober enough to be having this conversation as well. So get on with it, seal the deal, or whatever it’s called. I am a patient man, when it comes to you, but I am not waiting until your 26th to have another one of these conversations.”

Phainon gapes.

Mydei is staring at him with all the features of a drunk man– flushed eyes, flushed cheeks, the slight sway of his shoulders, but his eyes are clear as they always are. A trick of the light or a trick of the heart, he doesn’t know. But Phainon considers his options, pondering for a second, before throwing propriety out the window. Fuck it.

He kisses him, hard, blood orange and gin on his lips. He doesn’t like alcohol. Never will and never has, but this , this is addicting. Intoxicating. He could get drunk off Mydei alone. This is Phainon’s third kiss– all of his kisses have been Mydei, so he doesn’t really know how to compare, but his hands flit about, awkward.

He doesn’t know where to hold, doesn’t know where to look. His eyes? His nose? His lips? Or should he just keep his eyes shut, completely? That would be a waste, though. All of him is beautiful. He wants to treasure this. All of this.

“Phainon,” Mydei’s arms loop around his neck, dragging him down. “Ask me, already. Ask. With your words, not just your mouth or your tongue. It’s about time, is it not? I’m tired of waiting.”

“You could wait a little longer,” Phainon mutters against his lips. Hungry. He hasn’t eaten anything all day.

“Animal.” Mydei’s hisses as his hand comes to cover Phainon’s mouth. “You slobber all over me and you stink of gin. Confess while you’re sober. Anything else could wait.”

Phainon waves the thought away to lick Mydei’s palm, pressing a kiss to it instead, feather-light. “Mydei,” he starts, “Mydeimos. Love of my life.”

A snort.

“Would you do the honours of becoming my one and only?”

“I thought I was, already,” and he kisses him again, and Phainon laughs against his lips.

In the dark of their booth in a bar he doesn't care about, Phainon finally gets a boyfriend, he thinks. Maybe a boyfriend in name, just a label slapped onto what's already there. Maybe nothing much has changed. Not much has to, not much will.

He sighs, dreamy, as Mydei kisses his cheek, playful and satisfied all at once.

Getting to kiss him is a sweet bonus, though.

Phainon seemed like he wanted to apologize again, but their toaster-micowave-oven rang. “Just leave this to me,” Mydei said, getting up and turning away, “you owe me one, that’s all. Just take me out for lunch.”

The other had just stared, wide-eyed and earnest, looking like he’d just owed Mydei some life-saving debt, and that was when Mydei really did kick him out of the kitchen.

Mydei still remembers the day after. Phainon showed up to the cafe, sporting another horrid combination of bright orange and blue he’d worn, catching Mydei’s eye even as he waited patiently with the other customers for his shift to end.

He’d approached him after, a grin on his face as he bolted towards Mydei, bleary and tired and just slightly questioning the sudden closeness with his new roommate, dutifully reporting that his frappe monstrosity and rolls had somehow gotten professor Anaxa ( he even let him call him ‘Anaxa’, instead of ‘Anaxagoras’) to smile . Whether it was because of the quality of the food itself or because of Cipher’s tip didn’t matter, so long as his assignment was done.

Earnestly, Phainon had thanked him, casually hugging him in the staff room and then stepping back just as easily as he asked him out (to lunch). Mydei, caught in the whirlwind of it all, still reeling from the hug, barely blushing but definitely flustered, had just enough sense in him left to nod, before he was dumped into reality, sitting at a dingy fast-food restaurant that Phainon had sworn was his favourite.

And that was the first meeting of the two.

There was a symbol on his mother’s ring.

The symbol of Strife, apparently. A word that meant war, bloodshed, and death, one that was distinctly Kremnoan. It sat upon his mother’s pinky finger like a promise. It sat on her finger as a mark of her family.

And then, the ring was gone.

Mydei had noticed the fact after they’d moved. His mother was always the type to teach instead of instruct. If she wanted him to aid in chores or the like, she would show him how to do so, first. Normally he’d watch her slip off her ring, place it aside like a treasure, and then her hands would be filled with the metaphorical dirt, or the literal suds of soap, of dough and of cooking.

She hadn’t done that, after the move. Muscle memory came to slip off a ring made of air and not gold and she’d catch herself in the motion, laughing almost sadly, mourning what she had left behind.

It was an old memory, but one that stuck with him.

Another day, another time, his mother had done it again, and again, and again, the same slightly sad, slightly surprised expression. He’d asked her about it, then, on an off day between the time he’d started middle school and during the time he’d learned how to bleach-clean a shirt.

“My ring?” His mother questioned back, “What about it?”

The two were hunched over a little tub of bleach water. Two shirts, both his, both white, sank slowly in the warm acid water.

“It’s in Kremnos, isn’t it, mother?” Along with the journals and pictures and letters you used to keep of him, of my father, of your used-to-be husband.

She huffed, “It’s at the bottom of the sea, my son,” she said, a gentle, ringless hand settling on his head, “why do you ask? Oh, don’t touch that. The water’s hot.”

His mother always asked him that. Not just what he was doing but why.

“Isn’t it special?” He asked again, petulant, mindlessly sticking his pinky finger in the water.

“It once was, maybe,” she shrugged, “but it’s just a ring, now. Another thing to keep in Kremnos.”

Gently, she lifted his hand out the water, “Look, you’ve left your finger in, now it’s all crummy and wrinkled. We can’t have that. This is why you must use gloves as you wash.” She said, handing him a pair.

Distinctly, his mother’s own hands were bare as she submerged them under water.

“The water’s fine now, son. Come, have a try.”

He did, wordlessly, feeling lukewarm water settle into his skin, the bleach making his fingers shrivel almost as if rejecting him. He fished around to find a shirt, to scrub at it like his mother did.

“You see this?” She pointed, lifting one of the shirts out of the water, “It’s white. Or, well,  it used to be.” The shirt was off-white, slightly yellow from age or from an old spill or stain. A usual testament of its time, of casual sign of use.

“Sometimes, things just get old. They’re not broken yet, or unusable. Just old. Just no longer what we need,” she said, submerging the shirt underwater again.

“But we don’t throw them away, dear. We keep them somewhere else, until we make the effort to change them, or until we can spend the hour or so it takes to soak them in bleach. Until someone comes along who makes us want to bring up old things and renew what we thought was lost,” she smiled, once more, looking at him. But it wasn’t quite so sad.

“Can everything be washed like that?” He asked.

“Not with bleach, maybe,” she laughed, softly, “but nothing stays the same forever. Old things have meaning to new people. Old practices mean new things with new people.”

Slowly, Mydei lifted his own shirt out of the water, watching the suds slip off, slowly, taking away the stains, the discoloration, the age, the time along with it. His mother grinned as she walked away, washing her hands of the soap.

“I don’t have it in me to clean so often anymore,” she said, drying her hands off and silently looking at her own palms, “my hands are crummy and wrinkled, even without the bleach.”

She sighed, and Mydei didn’t think she was only talking about t-shirts anymore.

“But your hands are new, my son. Your hands have gloves as well. You don’t have to get shriveled up or ugly like mine.”

He tilted his head, frowning. “Your hands are well, mother.”

She grinned, “You think so?” He nodded.

His mother’s palms were large, large enough to knead a batch of dough, to ruffle his hair just so, large enough to cup his cheeks in both hands and pat his shoulder and hold his wrist, just gently, whenever he felt unsure.

Her palms were generous, always upturned and offering to neighbours, to children, to strangers down the street, always prepared to hold a fall when he felt shaky after a spar with Krateros. Warm to offer consolation, ample affection to hold him whenever he needed.

Her hands were strong enough to carry the life they had in Kremnos and rebuild it brick by brick through every relic, every book and waft of a smell. Every bit of furniture and moving box she’d unpacked and settled herself.

Her fingers were gentle as they carded through his hair with a brush or with her own digits, moving aside his bangs from where they fell on his face, or when twisting and braiding his hair. One, a long twist down and through the center or a smaller braid in front, a habit ingrained in his fingers.

But most importantly of all, her hands were hers , attached to the lovely, strong mother he’s always known. They could never be ugly or crummy or wrong, because they were his mother’s.

“Your hands are well,” he’d said again, even without a ring to adorn them his mother's hands would always be precious and kind.

Gorgo looked at her son, wide eyes almost indignant at how she’d described her hands, his own palms dutifully scrubbing at some old ratty shirt he hadn’t worn in years and there was no way to describe her heart but full , so very full of the love, of the joy of having a boy who loved and loves so much, so fiercely.

Her hand, imperfect, and lost, and no longer bearing the mark of her family, could only offer the barest bit of warmth as she carded through his hair, gentle, appreciative and loving, but he’d leaned into the touch regardless, a boyish, young look on his face.

What a wonderful thing it is, to be loved so gently. She kissed his forehead and his nose and he giggled, in the way sons do with their mothers, muttering ‘ it tickles!’ as he grinned.

Her hands bore scars and old marks. Regrets and lost, unlovely things.

But if they could hold him, still, her son, her boy. If they were enough to guide him to cook, to clean, to touch and to love.

Then maybe her hands, still, are well.

“You seem to be having fun,” Mydei says, descending the staircase as he leans against the doorframe.

Gorgo is sitting next to Phainon, still, a photobook in her lap. Phainon huffs, “Not as much as you were, up there. Going to the bathroom, was it? You were there for a solid half hour!”

He rolls his eyes, “You exaggerate. I was visiting my old room, as well. Did you miss me that much?”

“Nope!” Phainon replies, grinning wide, “Your mother makes for great company. You can go run off and reminisce in your old bedroom, Mydei.”

Mydei shoves at him playfully as Phainon laughs, Gorgo closes the picturebook, softly, and shakes her head.

“You boys really are too much,” she says, pinching both their cheeks as Phainon flails and Mydei rubs at the reddenned skin. “Mydeimos,” she continues, “have you found what you were looking for?”

He huffs from where he stands by Phainon, nodding gently.

“That’s good,” she grins, “It’s best I leave you to it, then. I’ll be off to the museum. You keep your spare with you, lock the door when you leave.”

Mydei’s eyes soften at the sight of his mother, smiling in approval and bright. She looks happier these days. He thinks they both do. “Be well, mother.”

She laughs, “Of course.”

Before she leaves Phianon strides over, taking both her hands in his. “Gorgo, I-” he pauses, looking back at Mydei, “There are many things that I’d like to say to you. But thank you. For everything. For allowing me your son. I can’t promise much, but-”

“There is nothing,” she cuts, “for you to thank me for, son.”

Gently, she pats his hair, making him lean down, instinctively, unable to see her expression. “I’m the one who should thank you, boy,” her voice sounds old, at once, old and ancient, like she’s lived through multiple lives and loss, “be well, okay? The both of you.”

Softly, she cradles both his cheeks, warm and loving at once and that is when he sees her expression, slightly teary, wholly accepting. Gratitude in the form of love, of care.

“And-” she pauses, almost afraid to ask as she whispers, close to his ear, “make my boy happy, please.”

Phainon’s heart thumps in his chest. Yet, his heart thumps out of it as well. His heart stands, by the dining table still, aching at the scene of his lover and mother and his world and his sun, his home and his other half.

Phainon thinks that he cannot be perfect, that he cannot promise much, but he can promise this, at least. He will swear it.

“For as long as he has me,” he whispers back, “I’ll love him. I promise you that.”

Gorgo huffs, a smile, a laugh, a sob all at once. “That is all I could ask.”

She lets go, patting his cheek, waving a goodbye to the both of them. “And before I forget,” she says as she stands by the doorway, halfway to leaving as she looks at Phainon, “I’d asked Chartonus to forge another spare of the keys. It’s by the drawer. Keep it on you, son.”

And then, the door clicks shut.

Mydei hadn’t been back to Kremnos since their move.

He didn’t hate the city, nor did he leave with any regrets. But maybe that was why he’d never returned. There weren’t even any ghosts to haunt him there.

He had no pull towards the city, towards the neighbourhoods or his old home. He felt for the culture, the history, the language, the things that mattered, still, to his mother, to his life in Okhema. But the old house, the old relics, the things they’d left behind– he didn’t feel the need to mourn a life he barely remembered.

Yet, he stood, still, in front of four walls in a neighbourhood that didn’t recognize him anymore. He stood, still, in front of a house that used to be home. This is the first time, the only time, he thinks, that he’ll ever return to this place.

He gripped the key in his hands, rusted from almost two decades of unuse, and he opened the door, to silence.

He coughed, slightly, a thick layer of dust permeating the house.

Mydei had told Phainon that his trip to Kremnos would take a few days— five, at most. It took about a day to make the trip and check-in to the place he’d rented, at least two days to feasibly move and flip through the house and a day to return to Okhema.

The house looked more packed than he remembered, boxes of old picturebooks and clothing, things she’d kept from the marriage but could not bear to bring.

He doesn’t know if he hates his father for what he's done. Whatever, wherever he might be today, Mydei holds no contempt. He only knows that his father was fined some amount, that he’d lost custody, and had moved away. Whether that meant he stayed in Kremnos or if he moved somewhere else is, frankly, no longer a concern for either him or his mother.

And so he digs through the boxes and the cabinets to look for an old ring, and he thinks of his new person and new memories and old tees. He thinks of washing away a past, of redefining family. He thinks of blue and white and how lovely he’d look with gold, and he thinks of his mother and his father and he prays for love that will last.

His heart thumps, slow, heady, but light, working through dust and through the day.

Stashed away unlike a treasure but more a secret is a ring, with the symbol of war, bloodshed, and death. To Kremnos, a symbol of royalty. To his mother, a symbol of family.

To him, a symbol of what could be. Of meaning stamped in gold, of a promise reforged.

He remembers the conversation that prompted this trip, a call with his mother as she was in Janusapolis looking to aid in another museum’s exhibition.

“And you’re marrying this boy, yes?” She’d questioned.

Mydei choked on his spit.

“Mydeimos?” His mother asked, worried, “are you alright? Don’t tell me you’re ill.”

“I’m-” he hacked, “I’m quite alright.” He blushed on the other end.

As embarrassing as it was to be outing himself to his mother, hiding such a large portion of his life (and hopefully future life) was frankly worse. He’s been more open to discussing such…feelings with his mother. It seemed to take the edge off her worry.

“It is my intention, yes, eventually to marry,” he admitted, face still hot, “but he hasn’t even confessed yet. I’d thought he reciprocated…” he muttered.

His mother hummed on the other end. “He loves you,” she says, conclusively, “I can assure that much, my son. Perhaps he’s only worried that you don’t reciprocate.”

Mydei frowned. Was that really it?

He’d thought he’d been quite forward with his feelings all this time. His invitations to spar, to dinner, his effort in taking care of the other at all times. It wasn’t that his actions weren’t enough, it was simply that Phainon didn’t want to see it as romantic. It was a refusal of acknowledgement, but not a refusal of there being something between them.

“And you haven’t confessed, dear?” She asked, breezily on the line.

“I haven’t,” he said, “I won’t.”

His mother hummed once more, not replying, but he knew she understood.

It was not that he didn’t love Phainon, obviously not, it was simply a question of when they’d meet in the middle. He loved him, imperfect and unwhole and entirely human. He loved him as a rival, a friend, roommate, an annoyance and everything in between.

He’s shown him that. That love. That same, unwavering, devotion. The only thing he’s missing is faith. The trust in himself to accept his heart, to allow himself this love, this next step.

He would love the man even if he’d never noticed. He’s only ever been waiting for him to ask.

“You intend to find my ring again?”

He breathes. “If you’ll allow me to.”

“Mydeimos,” she says, like reminding a child, like a mother, like he need not even ask, “there would be no greater joy.”

He’d asked for permission to keep it. To dunk it in proverbial bleach and watch as old meaning fell away, to see it give way to something kinder, something new. He hopes to keep it with him, awaiting whenever it is he might need it. Awaiting the day the man he’s already promised himself to will accept.

“You’ll be alone for quite some time,” his mother’s voice lilts, “but you will wait for him, yes?”

Mydei thinks of belonging.

He thinks of kind words and comforting touches, of an intimacy that always felt so casual, so easy. He thinks of a lonely path gaining another pair of footsteps. He thinks of routine, of a life built, of opportunities and companionship and a burden lightened just so. He thinks of hands growing crinkled with his own, scrubbing away suds, making ripples in a basin he thought he’d wash alone, forever.

He thinks of chance encounters, of bright eyes and kind smiles. He thinks of a home carved out in Okhema.

And he thinks, for once in his life, that there will be something he regrets, something he will miss, if he does not seize it.

He thinks that there could never be hesitance in his answer.

“Always.”

“This is…”

“My mother’s ring.”

After Gorgo had left, Mydei had been quiet.

Phainon was about to tease, about to ask him if he was simply suddenly sad once his mother departed but before he spoke Mydei had looked up, golden eyes blazing in a kind of quiet determination, and Phainon had immediately forgotten what he was to say.

He’d sat them both down, face to face at the dining table and slowly, he’d pulled out a velvet box.

The ring inside shone, bright, golden, and polished. Sat atop it was a symbol, one he’s seen from the hours he’s poured into learning his lover’s culture, the diagram of a love he’s devoted himself to, ever since they’d met then in college.

“It’s beautiful,” he mutters, enraptured.

This ring belonged– belongs to someone important. To Mydei, to his mother, to his heart.

Mydei looks at him, quiet, “It’s yours,” he replies, shy of breath.

Phainon’s head snaps towards him, almost disbelieving.

A symbol of his culture, of his love, of his mother. What is Mydei doing, giving such a thing away?

“Keep it, Phainon,” Mydei pushes the box towards him, innocently glinting in the light. And Phainon would be the only one to say so, but in that moment, Mydei had seemed meek.

Like offering a vulnerability, a weak spot, his greatest boon or weakness.

The box sits atop his mother’s table in his old, childhood home. The image of it hits hard. This is the inner sanctity of what he holds most dear. His mother, his past and now, in this box, his future.

It is the intensity of Mydei’s love that makes him shudder. Devotion so holistic it would be terrifying if not that he feels the same. That he’s loved so intensely for just as long, that he wants to devote himself just as entirely– to his family, to his mother, to the things he loves and cares about. To him. To all of him.

His heart hammers in his chest, loud and erratic. He is not afraid of the commitment. No, he is only afraid of the promise.

It is one thing to be accepted by his mother and it is another to be acknowledged as a part of his family. Not simply a worthy lover but a worthy partner, a worthy son, someone worthy to stay, to have and hold his back.

It is one thing to be loved for who he is and what he does. It is another to be loved so entirely.

He wants to deny it. He wants, immediately, to ignore himself. To say, again, that he is unready, unworthy, unlovable, that he is unsure and incomplete and that he wants, to be ignorant, to deny Mydei this love and he wants, to be selfish, and to beg for him to wait a little longer.

But then he looks at Mydei, really looks, and suddenly, his mouth is dry.

Because Mydei looks at him with devotion so earnest that he cannot deny it. He looks at him with acceptance so clear that there can be no doubts. Mydei looks at him like he is wholly worthy of love, and Phainon cannot feel anything but small in the face of its enormity.

“Mydei,” he whispers, “ Mydeimos. ”

“Phainon,” he replies. “Please. Will you take it?”

He is not offering a ring, Phainon thinks, but he is offering himself.

Devotion packaged in gold, materialized in a promise.

His heart bubbles into his throat.

“You want this.” He says, and does not ask, “You want me,” he whispers, why?

“I want you,” he mutters, “even if you do not want yourself.”

I love you, he means, in your entirety.

Phainon wants to reply with his own, impossibly cheesy, unbearably sweet confession. But really, his brain is tired of having to think so much. Of so many doubts, of so much waiting, of too many what-ifs and what-nots and all he can think, all he can feel, now, is the wanting.

If Phainon denies this ring, this advance, he knows that Mydei would wait, however heartbroken he might be, until Phainon is better, until he is worthy.

Instead, Phainon stands, and kisses him.

And Mydei gasps but there is no hesitation when he responds, a giggle in his mouth, an arm around his neck, laughter, incredulous, beautiful laughter bubbling in his chest that threatens to spill even as his tongue slips past and their teeth clack together.

It bubbles in his chest but he does not release it but Phainon knows, anyway because he moves in closer and picks his lover up, spinning and Phainon allows his own laughter to escape as Mydei blushes but does not let go, arms locked tight around his shoulders.

Mydei smiles like the sun, like a cat, pleased and beckoning, “Phainon,” he breathes with the remnants of a laugh, “ Phainon , you haven’t answered my question.”

“What question?” He blinks innocently. Like a dog wagging its tail after causing mischief. Like he’s excited over the prospect of doing as he likes.

Mydei flicks his forehead.

“You’re being dense.”

“I’m being myself.”

“Exactly so.”

“And here I thought you loved me as I am.”

“Making jokes, are we?” Mydei’s hands cradle his face as he’s lifted, still, by his thighs in his arms. “I want to hear it from you. I want to hear you say it until you believe it to be true. That I want you, Phainon. I will always want you and that ring–”

His grip tightens ever so slightly cradling his jaw.

“It is a reminder. From me, to you. That so long as gold glistens and the symbol of strife holds. I will fight for you. I will love you. Whatever, whoever you become.”

“Even if I were a dog?”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “I would love you even if you’d never known me.”

And Phainon laughs, a rich sound that takes up his whole chest, that rises like the sun, like heat and smoke, the motion of his heart and his breath pushing his head back as he spins, cradling the world in his orbit.

“I love you,” he says as they fall on the floor, when his arms have given way but he’s managed to cradle him, still, protecting his heart from most of the fall.

Mydei lays atop his chest huffing, the incredulous kind of laugh that comes only when you’re in love.

“No, listen. I adore you,” Phainon says again, hand carding through his hair, his left hand smudging slightly on the pigment of his eyeliner, and his right hand’s thumb dropping down to his bottom lip, prodding, before kissing his thumb with a smirk, “You’re impossible and wonderful and the best thing that’s ever happened to me. You keep me sane. You inspire me to be better for myself and for you. You make me a better man because you are so incredible yourself.”

“I love you,” he says, finishing his speech, “and I want you. I want to have you, for as long as you will want me. And because I know you, I hope, that means that you want me forever, too.”

Phainon peers up at Mydei through his bangs, through the framing curtain of white that sweeps over his eyes, the shadows accentuate the boldness of his eyes, the certainty of his gaze and the back light of the kitchen shines on him just so, brightening his smile and the room. Even the light itself makes way for the wonderful man that is his lover. As if the world itself loves his soul.

“I love you,” Mydei replies, “with all the words I know and do not know how to say. With all the time we have spent and will spend together. I love you, and I don’t think anything could ever change that.”

And he kisses him once more. Slow and bright and sweet and it’s like the world itself has finished its orbit, like returning to spring after winter, returning to what’s known and warm and loved because it is its nature to. Because Phainon will always gravitate towards Mydei and because their orbits will always align.

“You haven’t. Answered. The question.” Mydei huffs.

“Have I not praised you enough?”

“That is not what I asked. Flattery will get you nowhere.”

Phainon laughs, “Where else do I need to go? Yes, Mydei, love of my life, heart of my body, yes, I will accept the ring and cherish it and, if I may, loop a chain around it and keep it around my neck so that I may never have to take it off. Yes, Mydeimos. I want you, I want this, forever, too.”

Mydei huffs, satisfied and Phainon sits up, both of his lover’s things straddling his own.

“Can we get back to this, then? I was getting excited making out.” He says, hand resting innocently atop his thigh.

Mydei blinks, incredulous, at the man he’d just sworn himself to, and he combusts, red and heady and embarrassed but wanting all at once.

“Not in my mother’s house!”
